name: Design an Identity Provider with Single Sign-On
intent: Let a person sign in once and reach every company application, with tokens that apps verify on their own, keys that change without an outage, a logout that really ends sessions, stronger proof for risky actions, and separate customers kept apart.
codeTitle: a small identity provider with rotating keys and logout
finalIntro: One person signing in once, opening a second app, doing a risky action and logging out.
prompt: Design the identity provider for a business platform with 2,000 customer companies, 20 million users and 500 applications. People sign in once and open any app without signing in again. Apps must be able to prove who the user is, risky actions need a second factor, logging out must end access everywhere, and a customer can bring its own corporate login system.
functional: Sign a user in once and let them open other apps without another prompt (single sign-on)
Redirect users to the identity provider and back to an app with proof of who they are, using OpenID Connect and SAML
Issue signed tokens that apps can check without calling the provider
Rotate the signing keys on a schedule and in an emergency
Log out of every app (single logout) and revoke access from the back end
Ask for a second factor again when an app needs a stronger proof (step-up)
Let each customer company have its own users, policies and optionally its own upstream login system
nonFunctional: A sign-in with a valid session completes in under 300 ms, and a first sign-in in under 2 seconds
Handle a few thousand sign-ins per second at the Monday-morning peak, and tens of thousands of token renewals
Apps keep working for people who are already signed in even if the provider is down for a few minutes
A logout or an account lock reaches every app within seconds
Never accept a token from the wrong customer, the wrong app, or an unknown key
A key can be replaced with no sign-in failures, and a leaked key can be cut off within minutes

firstAttempt.text: Every application keeps its own user table and password page, and sets its own session cookie. To make this feel like single sign-on, teams copy users between applications by script and share a cookie encryption key between apps on the same domain.
limits: People type a password into 500 different pages, so there are 500 places to phish and 500 password stores to protect
Turning off a leaver or forcing a second factor means changing every app one by one
A shared cookie key means one app's weakness exposes all of them, and it does not work across domains or for third-party apps
There is no standard proof of who the user is, so each new app needs custom integration
No central record of who signed in where, and no way to end a session everywhere

steps.title: Move login to one place and keep a single sign-on session
steps.problem: When every app owns its own passwords, people sign in 500 times, and the company cannot enforce one policy or switch off a leaver in one place.
steps.fix: Apps stop handling passwords. When an app has no session, it redirects the browser to the identity provider with its client id, the address to come back to, a random state value, a nonce, and a PKCE challenge. The provider shows the one login page and, on success, creates a single sign-on session: a record in a session store and a secure, HTTP-only cookie on the provider's own domain, with an idle timeout and an absolute limit such as 8 hours. The next app that redirects the browser finds the cookie, skips the prompt and sends the browser straight back with a short-lived, single-use authorization code.
steps.tradeoff: One login page to harden, one place to apply password and lock-out rules, and no extra prompts after the first. The provider is now critical to everything and a stolen session cookie opens many apps, so the session store, its cookie settings and its timeouts need the most care in the system.

steps.title: Issue signed tokens that apps verify by themselves
steps.problem: The app must learn who the user is from the browser, which could say anything, and asking the provider on every request would make the provider a bottleneck for all 500 apps.
steps.fix: The app's back end swaps the authorization code for an ID token and an access token at the provider's token endpoint, sending the PKCE verifier and its own credential. Each token is a signed statement: issuer, subject (a stable user id), audience (which app it is for), expiry a few minutes ahead, when and how the user signed in (auth_time and the authentication level), and the nonce. The provider signs with a private key and publishes the matching public keys at a JWKS address. Apps fetch and cache those keys and check the signature, issuer, audience and expiry locally. SAML does the same with a signed XML assertion posted through the browser.
steps.tradeoff: Apps verify tokens with no network call, so the provider's load depends on sign-ins and renewals rather than on every request. A token cannot be taken back once issued, so its lifetime is a trade between load and how long a stolen or revoked token keeps working, and apps must check audience and issuer strictly.

steps.title: Rotate signing keys without breaking a single sign-in
steps.problem: A key that never changes is a bigger prize and a bigger risk, but swapping it in one step makes every cached key set and every token in flight invalid at once.
steps.fix: Every token names the key that signed it (kid). A rotation job runs on a schedule, such as every 90 days: it creates the new key pair in a hardware-backed key store, publishes the new public key in the JWKS first, waits longer than apps cache the key set, then starts signing with it. The old public key stays published until the last token it signed has expired, plus a margin for clock skew. An app that sees an unknown kid refetches the key set once, with a rate limit. For an emergency the old key is removed from the set immediately.
steps.tradeoff: Rotation becomes routine and invisible, and a leaked key stops working once removed. The key set must be served with sensible cache headers and be highly available, the schedule needs monitoring, and an emergency removal deliberately fails every token signed with that key, so people must sign in again.

steps.title: Log out everywhere, and revoke from the back end
steps.problem: Logging out of the provider ends only its own cookie. Every app still holds a session or an unexpired token, and the same is true when an account is locked or a password is reset.
steps.fix: For each single sign-on session the provider records a session id and which apps received tokens for it. On logout, lock or reset it puts one signed logout token (session id and subject) per app onto a queue, and a worker posts each one directly to the app's back-channel logout address, with retries and backoff. The app ends its local session for that session id and remembers the id as revoked until its tokens would have expired. Front-channel logout, with hidden pages in the browser, is kept as a best effort only, because browsers block and close such pages. Sensitive APIs can also introspect a token to ask whether it is still active.
steps.tradeoff: Logout works even when the browser is gone and takes effect in seconds. It needs every app to implement the endpoint and a revoked-session check, delivery can still fail for an app that is down, and the short token lifetime from the previous step remains the final safety net.

steps.title: Ask for more proof only when an action needs it (step-up)
steps.problem: Asking for a second factor at every sign-in annoys people, but a password alone is too weak for payroll, admin screens or changing a bank account.
steps.fix: Tokens record the authentication level reached (acr) and when the user last proved themselves (auth_time). An app that guards a risky action states what it needs, such as multi-factor within the last 5 minutes. If the token is not good enough, it redirects to the provider with the required level and a maximum age. The provider asks for a passkey or a one-time code from the MFA service, upgrades the existing single sign-on session, and returns a fresh token with the higher level. The provider can also demand a second factor on its own for a new device or an unusual location.
steps.tradeoff: Strong proof is requested exactly where it matters and the normal flow stays smooth. Apps must ask for the right level and check the claim, the second-factor attempts need rate limits and a safe recovery path, and the recovery path then becomes the weakest link to watch.

steps.title: Keep customers apart, and federate to their own login systems
steps.problem: Each customer company wants its own users and rules, and many want staff to sign in with their own corporate system. A token from one customer must never be accepted by another's apps.
steps.fix: Make the tenant a first-class part of everything. Each tenant has its own issuer address, its own signing keys, its own policies (second factor required, session length, allowed domains) and its own user directory, in a tenant settings store. Apps accept only the issuer of their tenant. A tenant can connect an upstream login system over OpenID Connect or SAML: the provider works out which tenant a person belongs to from their email domain, sends them upstream, maps the returned claims to its own stable user id (not the email address), creates the user on first sight, and then issues its own token. Leavers are removed through a provisioning feed.
steps.tradeoff: Isolation is strong, so a key or a mistake in one tenant does not touch the rest, and customers keep control of their people. There is a lot more configuration, one rotation schedule per tenant, and claim mapping that can be wrong in subtle ways, such as trusting an email address that an upstream system does not verify.

failures.scenario: The identity provider is down for ten minutes
failures.impact: Nobody can start a new sign-in, and a bad design would also reject every request because tokens can no longer be checked.
failures.answer: Apps verify tokens against their cached key set and keep their local sessions, so people already signed in carry on. Only new sign-ins and renewals fail. The provider runs in several zones with a replicated session store, the key set is served through a CDN, and the apps' renewal logic retries with backoff instead of sending everyone back to the login page at once.

failures.impact: Anyone holding it can mint a valid token for any user of that tenant, including an administrator.
failures.answer: The key is removed from the key set at once and a new one is made active, so forged and genuine tokens signed with the old key fail alike. Sessions are revoked, users sign in again, and the audit log is searched for tokens issued in the window. Keeping private keys in a hardware-backed store, so that they cannot be copied out, makes this rare, and per-tenant keys keep the damage to one tenant.

failures.scenario: A back-channel logout message cannot be delivered
failures.impact: An app was down, so it never learns about the logout, and the former user still has access there.
failures.answer: The queue retries with growing delays, and messages that still fail go to a dead-letter queue for an alert. Because the message names a session id, delivering it twice is harmless. The exposure of an app that missed it is limited by its token lifetime, and sensitive apps check a token's session against the provider when they act.

failures.scenario: A session cookie or token is stolen and replayed
failures.impact: The thief acts as the user in every app the session reaches, without knowing the password.
failures.answer: Cookies are secure and HTTP-only with a short idle timeout and an absolute limit, and tokens are short-lived. Risk checks watch for a session that suddenly appears in a new country or on a new device, which triggers a step-up or a revocation. Sensitive actions demand fresh multi-factor proof anyway, and an admin or the user can end all sessions with one action.

failures.scenario: An app rejects valid tokens just after a key rotation
failures.impact: Users see errors in one app only, because its cached key set does not contain the new key yet or its clock runs behind.
failures.answer: The new key is published before it is used, longer than any app caches the set. An unknown kid triggers one rate-limited refetch, and apps allow about a minute of clock skew on expiry and issue times. A dashboard that counts signature failures by app and key id shows the problem within minutes.

alternatives.title: Which protocol to speak

options.name: OpenID Connect
options.pro: JSON tokens, simple for web, mobile and APIs, and the protocol most new apps expect
options.con: Needs care to validate every claim, and older enterprise software may not support it

options.name: SAML 2.0
options.pro: Universal in older enterprise and government software
options.con: Verbose signed XML, harder to implement safely, and awkward for mobile apps and APIs

options.name: Both from one provider
options.pro: Every app and every customer's upstream system can connect
options.con: Two code paths, two sets of security pitfalls to maintain

alternatives.pick: OpenID Connect by default, with SAML offered for the apps and customers that still need it.

alternatives.title: How apps check a token

options.name: Signed token checked locally
options.pro: No call to the provider, so it scales with apps and survives short outages
options.con: Cannot be revoked until it expires

options.name: Opaque token with introspection
options.pro: Can be revoked instantly, and the provider sees every use
options.con: One call per request, and the provider becomes a bottleneck and a single point of failure

options.name: Short signed token plus a revoked-session check
options.pro: Local in the common case, and revocation is quick through logout messages
options.con: Slightly more logic in every app

alternatives.pick: Short signed tokens verified locally, with back-channel logout, and introspection only for the most sensitive APIs.

alternatives.title: How logout reaches the apps

options.name: Front-channel (hidden pages in the browser)
options.con: Blocked by browsers, fails when the tab is closed, and cannot be retried

options.name: Back-channel (server to server)
options.pro: Reliable, works with no browser open, and can be retried
options.con: Each app needs a reachable endpoint and must handle repeats

options.name: Only short token lifetimes
options.pro: Nothing to build in the apps
options.con: Access lasts until expiry, and a short expiry means a lot more renewals

alternatives.pick: Back-channel as the main path, short lifetimes as the safety net, and front-channel only as a bonus.

alternatives.title: How tenants are kept apart

options.name: One issuer and one key for all
options.con: A tenant claim inside the token is the only wall, so one bug or leaked key affects everybody

options.name: A separate issuer and keys per tenant
options.pro: A leaked key or a mix-up stays inside one tenant, and a customer can bring its own key
options.con: Thousands of key sets to rotate and monitor

options.name: A separate deployment for each large customer
options.pro: Full isolation, including load and data location
options.con: Costly, and every fix must roll out many times

alternatives.pick: A separate issuer and keys per tenant on shared infrastructure, and dedicated deployments only for the largest or most regulated customers.

roles.label: Browsers
roles.description: Where people sign in and carry the redirects between apps and the provider.

roles.label: Login endpoints
roles.description: The identity provider's authorize and token endpoints, and customers' own login systems.

roles.label: Apps and checks
roles.description: The apps that trust the provider, and the second-factor service.

roles.label: State
roles.description: Sessions, signing keys and tenant settings.

quiz.question: A user signs in to the payroll app at payroll.example.com. They then open the wiki, a different app at wiki.partner.net, which has no session for them. They are not asked for a password. What lets the wiki skip the login prompt?
options: The wiki reads the payroll app's session cookie, since both apps share the same encryption key for session cookies
The wiki asks the payroll app's back end whether this browser has a live session, and trusts the answer it gets back
The wiki redirects to the identity provider, which sees its own session cookie and sends back a single-use code
The browser stores the user's password after the first login and fills it in on the wiki's own login page every time
quiz.explanation: The identity provider has its own session and cookie on its own domain, so any app that redirects there is answered without a prompt. Cookies are not shared across domains, and asking another app or storing a password are not how single sign-on works.

quiz.question: A leaver's account is disabled at 09:00. Access tokens last 60 minutes and apps verify them locally. HR wants all access to stop within a few minutes. There are 20 million users, many online all day. What is the best approach?
options: Send a signed back-channel logout message with the session id to each app, and keep access tokens short-lived too
Shorten every access token to 5 minutes and rely only on expiry, which means 12 renewals per hour for each active user
Have every app call the provider's introspection endpoint on every request, to ask whether the token is still active
Rotate the provider's signing key at once, which makes every token it has issued fail validation in every app
quiz.explanation: Back-channel logout reaches each app in seconds without a browser, and the short lifetime covers an app that missed the message. Expiry alone is slow or costs 12 renewals per hour per user. Introspection on every request makes the provider a bottleneck, and a key rotation logs out everybody, not just the leaver.

quiz.question: A signing key rotation signs tokens with the new key as soon as it is created, and the key set is published at the same time. Apps cache the key set for 10 minutes. For 10 minutes after each rotation, a share of requests fails signature checks. How should the rotation be changed?
options: Set the apps' key set cache to 0 seconds, so that every token check fetches the current keys from the provider directly
Publish the new public key first, wait longer than apps cache it, then sign with it, and keep the old key until its tokens expire
Sign each token with both keys at once, so that apps holding either version of the key set can validate it either way
Remove the old key from the set as soon as the new one is active, so that no token signed by it is ever accepted again
quiz.explanation: Apps must know the new key before any token uses it, and old tokens must stay verifiable until they expire. A zero-second cache would send the load of every check to the provider. A token has one signature, so signing with two keys is not how it works, and removing the old key at once breaks tokens in flight.
